questions.prompt: Relations R (1000 blocks) and S (500 blocks) are joined with a block nested-loop join using 502 buffer blocks, with S as the outer relation. Roughly how many block transfers are required?
questions.explanation: With 500 blocks of S plus buffers to spare, S fits in memory entirely: read S once (500) and R once (1000) = 1500 transfers. The quadratic 500,000 figure applies only when the outer relation must be processed in chunks.

questions.prompt: Which transformation is a valid equivalence rule used by a query optimizer?

options.text: Replacing an outer join with an inner join unconditionally
Pushing a projection below a selection that references the projected-away column
Reordering aggregation before grouping
Pushing a selection below a join when the predicate uses only that relation's attributes

questions.explanation: Selection pushdown is the classic heuristic: filtering early shrinks the intermediate result feeding the join. The others change query semantics — a projection cannot discard a column a later predicate needs.

questions.prompt: External merge sort is used on a 100-block file with 10 buffer blocks. How many initial sorted runs are produced?
questions.explanation: The sort phase fills all 10 buffer blocks, sorts them in memory and writes each as a run, giving ceil(100/10) = 10 runs. The merge phase then combines them, using 9 blocks for input and 1 for output.

questions.prompt: The selectivity of a predicate is best described as:

options.text: The number of indexes the predicate can use
The fraction of tuples that satisfy the predicate
The number of disk blocks the predicate reads
The CPU cost of evaluating the predicate

questions.explanation: Selectivity is the expected fraction of rows passing the filter, estimated from catalogue statistics such as histograms. Low selectivity favours an index scan; high selectivity favours a full scan.

questions.prompt: For an equijoin where the join attribute of S has a B+ tree index, indexed nested-loop join is preferable to block nested-loop join when:

options.text: The outer relation is small and the index is selective
Both relations are very large and unsorted
No index exists on either relation
The join predicate is an inequality

questions.explanation: Cost is roughly (blocks of outer) + (tuples of outer × index lookup cost), so few outer tuples and a selective index keep it cheap. With a huge outer relation, the per-tuple probes dominate and a hash or merge join wins.

questions.prompt: Why does a query optimizer typically consider only left-deep join trees?

options.text: Bushy trees cannot use indexes
They are the only trees that produce correct results
They keep the search space manageable and allow pipelining of intermediate results
They always produce the globally optimal plan

questions.explanation: Restricting to left-deep shapes cuts the plan space dramatically and suits pipelined execution, since one input to each join is always a base relation. It is a heuristic, so the true optimum may be missed.

questions.prompt: Relations R and S have 1000 and 2000 tuples. The join attribute is a foreign key in R referencing the primary key of S. How many tuples does the natural join produce, at most?
questions.explanation: Each R tuple matches at most one S tuple, since the referenced attribute is a primary key. So the result has at most |R| = 1000 tuples — exactly 1000 if no foreign key value is NULL.

questions.prompt: In hash join, what is the purpose of the partitioning (build) phase?

options.text: To sort both relations on the join attribute
To split both relations into buckets so matching tuples land in the same bucket
To eliminate duplicate tuples before joining
To build a B+ tree index on the smaller relation

questions.explanation: Hashing the join attribute of both inputs guarantees that any pair that could match falls into the same partition, so each partition can be joined independently in memory.

questions.prompt: Materialization differs from pipelining in query evaluation because materialization:

options.text: Requires the query to be read-only
Always uses less disk I/O
Writes each operator's intermediate result to disk before the next operator reads it
Can only be used with sort-based operators

questions.explanation: Materialization stores intermediates, costing extra I/O but simplifying execution and enabling reuse. Pipelining streams tuples straight into the next operator, avoiding that write — though blocking operators like sort must materialize anyway.

questions.prompt: A cost-based optimizer relies primarily on which source of information to choose a plan?

options.text: The number of users connected to the database
The order in which tables appear in the FROM clause
The physical order of rows on disk only
Catalogue statistics such as relation sizes, distinct value counts and histograms

questions.explanation: Cost-based optimization estimates the cost of candidate plans from catalogue statistics. This is why stale statistics cause bad plans — and why running ANALYZE often fixes a sudden regression.
